verdict: Caution: lend selectively to secondary re-rollers with firm offtake and tight power/coal cover; avoid merchant re-rollers selling into a soft local market.
title: Bokaro Iron & Steel: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Bokaro steel is two very different businesses sitting in one city.** The anchor is SAIL's Bokaro Steel Plant, a large integrated works whose employees are still being given Amazon gift coupons ahead of Diwali [1] — that tells you the plant is running and paying wages, but says nothing about its order book. Around it sits the secondary re-rolling belt: small units that buy billets or scrap, melt and roll into TMT bars and structurals, and sell into local construction and the Jharkhand-Bihar trade. **Cash is made on the spread between input (scrap, billet, coking coal, power) and the TMT price, not on volume alone.**

## Where value and cash sit
**The working-capital cycle is the whole credit story.** Inventory sits as scrap/billet, then WIP, then finished bars; debtors are typically 30-60 days in trade. So when a proposal lands, check the inventory days and debtor days against the last two years, and if debtor days have stretched while sales are flat, ask who the new buyers are and whether they are paying. **Capex is lumpy and mostly furnace/rolling-mill upgrades — fund only against a demonstrated order book, never against optimism.**

## What has changed now
**The local demand signal is mixed and the data call is Caution.** Jharkhand GST collections fell 0.2% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D] — a real local stress signal. Offsetting that, Jharkhand electricity demand rose 15.2% Apr-to-date versus India's +9.5% [D], and India-wide IIP for NIC 24 (basic metals) is +2.4% YoY, +3.4% Apr-to-date [D]. **Power is the swing input here: Bokaro's coal stocks have fallen to 'three days' [3], so when a proposal lands, check the unit's power source and coal cover; if it depends on grid power with no captive arrangement, ask for the last six months of power bills.** Peer results are strong but not uniform — JSW Steel's Q2 FY27 net profit was Rs.5,279 crore versus Rs.1,623 crore a year earlier [4], while Kirloskar Ferrous saw revenue up 17% y-o-y to INR 2,046.7 crore but margins eroded by coking coal and rupee depreciation [6]. **Read that as: volumes are fine, spreads are not.**

## Who to pursue, who to avoid
**Pursue secondary re-rollers with a tied buyer** — a unit selling a defined share of output to a government contractor or a branded TMT distributor, with captive or contracted power. **Avoid pure merchant re-rollers selling into the open local trade with no offtake agreement**, and avoid anyone whose expansion is funded by the promoter's other group entities. Note the JSW Steel Parvatpur coal-block landowner protest over jobs [2] — local land and employment friction can stall a project; if a borrower's site is near disputed land, ask for the lease/patta and the panchayat no-objection.

## Structure, covenants and early warning
**Take monthly stock and debtor statements, not quarterly.** Structure as a cash-credit with a drawing power tied to paid stock and book debts, plus a monthly power-bill and GST-return covenant. **Watch:** GST filings vs bank credits (monthly) — a gap of more than one return cycle means stop fresh disbursal; coal/power cover (weekly) — below a week's cover, ask for the sourcing plan; debtor ageing (monthly) — any single buyer above 25% of receivables, ask for the contract; and rolling-mill utilisation (monthly) — a fall below the borrower's own six-month average, ask for the order book. **Sources are thin on Bokaro-specific secondary steel data; lean on first principles and the peer set above.**

below one week's cover -> ask for sourcing plan and captive backup
single buyer above 25% of receivables -> ask for the offtake contract
below borrower's own six-month average -> ask for order book
rising while sales flat -> ask who the new buyers are
